blocks.text: In these isomers, identical ligands are present at either adjacent (90° angle, cis) or opposite (180° angle, trans) positions. This is common in square planar (e.g., [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]) and octahedral complexes (e.g., [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]).

The cis and trans isomers of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] are shown in Figure 18.11. In cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (cisplatin), the chlorine atoms are adjacent to each other at the angle of 90° in the square complex but in trans-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] (transplatin), they are opposite to each other at an angle of 180°. The properties of these geometrical isomers are different. It is interesting to know that cisplatin is used as an anti-cancer drug, while transplatin does not show such property.

blocks.alt: Two square-planar Pt complexes drawn on a dashed square. cis-platin: the two Cl at the left corners and the two NH3 at the right corners, so the Cl atoms are next to each other. trans-platin: Cl at the back left and front right, NH3 at the back right and H3N at the front left, so the Cl atoms are opposite each other.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.11: The geometrical isomers, cisplatin and transplatin (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.11).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 18.11 leaves out the central platinum atom; Pt is drawn at the centre above.

In transplatin, the individual bond dipoles of the identical ligands are pointed in opposite direction and cancel each other, making the molecule nonpolar. In cisplatin, the similar individual bond moments do not cancel out, resulting in a non-zero dipole moment that makes it polar.

blocks.title: Interesting Information
blocks.text: Cisplatin, or cis-diamminedichloroplatinum(II), is a landmark inorganic anticancer drug. Its discovery was accidental, found when platinum electrodes inhibited bacterial cell division. It specifically targets rapidly dividing cancer cells by entering the cell and undergoing ligand exchange, where water replaces its chloride ions. The "activated" drug then binds to guanine bases in DNA, creating cross-links that link the double helix. This structural damage prevents DNA replication, triggering programmed cell death (apoptosis).

[Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]³⁺ is an [MA₄B₂] type octahedral complex. The cis and trans isomers of [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]³⁺ are shown in Figure 18.12. In the cis isomer, the two H₂O ligands occupy adjacent positions at a 90° angle with respect to each other, while in the trans isomer, they occupy opposite positions at a 180° angle to each other.

blocks.alt: Under the heading OCTAHEDRAL COMPLEX ION, two drawings of [Co(NH3)4(H2O)2]3+, each a yellow square plane through Co with one ligand above and one below. cis-isomer: one H2O above the plane and the other at a corner of the plane, 90 degrees apart. trans-isomer: the two H2O at opposite corners of the plane, 180 degrees apart; NH3 above and below.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.12: The geometrical isomers, [Co(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]³⁺ (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.12, drawn as its two isomers).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 18.12 shows four drawings, as if there were four isomers. Drawings (i), (ii) and (iv) are all the same cis isomer (the two H₂O at 90°) and (iii) is the trans isomer (180°). An [MA₄B₂] octahedral complex has only two geometrical isomers, cis and trans, as drawn above.
